
Nothing here is a finding about ecology. The point is that once the tables
share a format, the same few lines of code run across all of them, and the
species behave like items: each has a prevalence (how many units hold it) and
a detectability (how often a survey finds it where it is). The figures are
computed by `analysis/figures_data.R` in the repository and redrawn here from
its output.

```{=html}
<div class="eco-figs">
  <div class="figure">
    <p class="ttl">Species as items</p>
    <div class="legend"><span style="--sw:var(--c1)">Los Lagos carnivores (4)</span><span style="--sw:var(--c2)">Pampas birds (43)</span><span style="--sw:var(--c3)">New River fish (74)</span></div>
    <svg id="f1" viewBox="0 0 520 340" role="img" aria-labelledby="f1t"><title id="f1t">Scatter of per-survey detection rate against naive occupancy for 121 species across three tables</title></svg>
    <p class="cap">Each dot is one species in one community table. Naive occupancy is the share of units with at least one detection; detection rate is the share of surveys that detected it. Fish species are found in 8% of surveys on average but a third of watersheds; the Pampas birds are rarer per survey still.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="figure">
    <p class="ttl">What a detection model adds</p>
    <div class="legend"><span style="--sw:var(--c1)">Los Lagos carnivores</span><span style="--sw:var(--c2)">Pampas birds, first season</span><span style="--sw:var(--ink-3)">Baird's tapir</span></div>
    <svg id="f2" viewBox="0 0 520 340" role="img" aria-labelledby="f2t"><title id="f2t">Estimated occupancy against naive occupancy for 24 species; every point lies above the identity line</title></svg>
    <p class="cap">A constant-probability occupancy model (<code>unmarked::occu</code>, ψ ~ 1, p ~ 1) fit to each species. Estimated occupancy exceeds naive occupancy for all 24 species, by 0.11 at the median. Dot size is per-survey detection probability p. The Pampas estimates sit at 1.0 because ten sites and p near 0.1 cannot pin ψ down; that is the sample-floor question in one picture.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="figure">
    <p class="ttl">Effort is a covariate, not a nuisance</p>
    <svg id="f3" viewBox="0 0 520 340" role="img" aria-labelledby="f3t"><title id="f3t">Median number of fish species detected per watershed-year by number of collections, with interquartile band</title></svg>
    <p class="cap">New River fish: species detected in a watershed-year against the number of collections that year (<code>obs_effort</code>). The median climbs from 7 species at one collection to about 17 at four or more. A HUC-year with one collection is a survey with low p, not a depauperate watershed.</p>
  </div>
  <div class="figure">
    <p class="ttl">A capture history read as a longitudinal item</p>
    <div class="legend"><span style="--sw:var(--c1)">first capture</span><span style="--sw:var(--c2)">recapture</span></div>
    <svg id="f4" viewBox="0 0 520 340" role="img" aria-labelledby="f4t"><title id="f4t">Captures of Plain-crested Elaenia per session, split into first captures and recaptures</title></svg>
    <p class="cap">Plain-crested Elaenia, nine sessions. The <code>period</code> column is the CJS time axis; recaptures accumulate as marked birds survive, and four histories end early with <code>obs_removed = 1</code>. The same table feeds <code>marked::crm</code> or NIMBLE's <code>dCJS</code> after one pivot.</p>
  </div>
</div>
```

The same two quantities, prevalence and detectability, are what an item
response model estimates for an item as difficulty and discrimination. The
analogy is not exact, since the ecological models put the "person" effect on
a latent occupancy state rather than a continuous trait, but it is close
enough that the tooling built for one transfers to the other, which is the
bet this project is making.
